title: Elements of Drama Warm-Up
walt: Identify and use the elements of drama through online drama games.
success: I can name at least three elements of drama.
I can use two elements of drama in a short improvisation.
wp: who you are pretending to be
where you are and what is happening
brain: Which element makes a freeze frame feel dramatic?
How can voice alone change the mood of one line?
Why does drama need contrast?

teach.title: Mini-lesson — Elements (App. A)
teach.body: Recap the 10 elements of drama: role, situation, voice, movement, space, time, tension, mood, focus, contrast.
teach.tip: Share App. A on screen. Keep it tight and clearly labelled.

teach.title: Re-teach with a student example
teach.body: Spotlight one volunteer. Name the elements you see. Tighten the use of voice and tension together.
teach.tip: Keep demos under two minutes so students get maximum doing time.

sequence: Call a word (celebration, storm, market) — students freeze in a pose that shows it. Gallery view; spotlight 3–4 each round.
Recap App. A — role, situation, voice, movement, space, time, tension, mood, focus, contrast. Share on screen; keep labels clear.
On mute, cameras on: 30–45 sec moment (mysterious box / waiting for big news) using at least two named elements. Drop situations in chat. No breakouts.
Spotlight one volunteer; name elements; tighten voice and tension.
Spotlight performances one at a time; class names elements in chat. Mute other mics.
Recap elements + exit ticket. Preview Lesson 2 — a short history of drama.
model: Perform a 20–30 sec mini-scene live, naming the two elements as you go: “watch for voice and tension here.”
watch: Drama warm-up & improv games · National Theatre / BBC Teach (~3 min)
exit: A. Phone call with fantastic news — react and reply
B. Mystery package at the door — open it on camera
C. Winning a strange competition — thank-you speech
resources: Webcam + mic · App. A on screen · element list pinned in chat
notes:
Appendix A on screen. Camera Freeze → elements mini-lesson → solo build → re-teach voice/tension → spotlight shares → 30-sec exit ticket.

Whole-class week — no breakouts yet.

title: A Short History of Drama
walt: Understand how drama has changed across time, and what a monologue and a soliloquy are.
success: I can describe one feature of drama from at least two time periods.
I can explain the difference between a monologue and a soliloquy.
wp: one character speaks to someone or the audience
private thoughts spoken aloud, usually alone
group that helped tell the story in Greek theatre
brain: Why did Greek actors wear masks?
How is a soliloquy different from chatting to a friend on stage?
What stayed the same from Greek theatre to filming at home?

teach.title: Timeline, part 1 (App. B)
teach.body: Ancient Greek theatre & medieval mystery/morality plays — two or three key facts each.
teach.tip: Keep each era memorable, not exhaustive. Share App. B on screen.

teach.title: Timeline, part 2 + mono vs soliloquy
teach.body: Elizabethan/Shakespearean & modern/digital drama (App. B). Introduce monologue vs soliloquy with App. C.
teach.tip: Act the same line both ways so the difference is obvious.

sequence: Call an era — masked Greek actor, medieval town-square player, Shakespearean actor, modern film star — students pose. Ask 2–3 to explain a choice.
App. B: Ancient Greek & medieval — 2–3 key facts each.
Pose or mime one feature per era so far; drop one fact in chat. Read a few aloud. No breakouts.
Elizabethan/Shakespearean & modern/digital + monologue vs soliloquy (App. C).
Independently jot 2–3 character ideas for a later monologue or soliloquy. Spotlight a few — mono or soliloquy? Quiet thinking first.
Recap mono vs soliloquy + exit ticket. Preview Lesson 3 — drama across cultures (first breakouts!).
model: Say one line twice: first as a monologue (to someone), then as a soliloquy (private thoughts, alone). Ask the class to spot the difference.
watch: Shakespeare’s Theatre (the Globe) · BBC Teach (~4 min) · youtube.com/watch?v=D1rbtHchv1g
exit: A. Masked Greek actor announces huge news to the city
B. Soliloquy: alone, deciding something big
C. Shakespearean town crier announces tomorrow’s event
resources: App. B History Timeline · App. C Monologue vs Soliloquy (on screen)
notes: Appendices B & C. Act the same line both ways. Character seeds feed Weeks 3–10 — no single right answer yet.

title: Drama Across Cultures
walt: Describe how drama communicates ideas and helps continue and revitalise culture.
success: I can describe one way a performance communicated meaning.
I can explain why storytelling matters to a culture.
wp: shared beliefs, stories and ways of life
a story passed down through generations
clever character who outwits a stronger foe
bring new life and energy to something
brain: What feelings did the performance communicate?
Why might this story matter to its culture?
Which story pattern could inspire your own piece?

teach.title: Teach + view storytelling clip
teach.body: Play the chosen storytelling/drama clip(s). Pause to ask: what is happening, and what ideas or feelings are being communicated?
teach.tip: Share screen with audio. Pre-test the link; have a backup clip ready. Preview for cultural appropriateness.

teach.title: Character & situation (App. D)
teach.body: Use App. D patterns to choose a character + situation — from a culture, folktale, history, or an original idea. Invite stories from students’ own backgrounds.
teach.tip: First breakouts this week — pin two questions in each room; clear time limit + 2-min warning.

sequence: One-sentence prompt; volunteers add a sentence (aloud or chat) to build a class story. Read chat additions aloud.
Play storytelling clip; pause for meaning and feeling.
Think-pair-share: what did it communicate, and why might the story matter to its culture? Pin both questions.
Patterns for character + situation; invite own-culture inspiration.
Independently choose character + situation; note where inspiration came from. Follow up anyone still undecided.
Exit ticket. Character + situation idea due at the start of Lesson 4.
model: Model answering “what did this communicate?” aloud, citing voice/movement/situation — then show how App. D helps lock a character + situation.
watch: Storytelling traditions around the world · TED-Ed / ABC Education (teacher-selected 1–2 clips)
exit: A. Opening of a folktale from your family or culture
B. Wise elder passing on one important lesson
C. Hero discovers something amazing
resources: 1–2 vetted culture clips · App. D Character Shortlist · breakout rooms (pairs)
notes: Appendix D. Breakout debut — pre-assign rooms, pin questions, pop into a couple of rooms to settle the routine.

title: Building Your Character
walt: Build a character through role, situation and voice.
success: I can describe my character’s role and situation.
I can find a voice and posture for my character.
wp: answering questions in role as your character
who you are pretending to be
how your body shows the character
brain: What does your character want most right now?
How would they walk into a room?
Which App. F question reveals the most?

teach.title: Hot-seating demo (App. F)
teach.body: Recap role, situation, voice. Demonstrate hot-seating — answer in role for about a minute using an App. F prompt.
teach.tip: Ask a volunteer to interview you in role so pairs see the format.

teach.title: Into the planning template (App. E)
teach.body: Show how to turn hot-seat answers into the Monologue Planning Template — character, situation and voice.
teach.tip: Keep a copy of templates so work isn’t lost if a student drops out.

sequence: Move on camera as characters you call — queen, trickster, giant, animal. Discuss how movement shows role.
Answer in role ~1 min with App. F; volunteer interviews you.
Pairs take turns hot-seating each other’s character with App. F prompts. Rotate rooms so both get a turn.
Transfer answers onto App. E — character, situation, voice.
Independently finalise character, situation and voice on the planning template.
Share character in one sentence + exit ticket. Preview Lesson 5 — finding the key moment.
model: Volunteer asks you one question; answer in role for ~30 sec with committed voice and posture.
watch: Hot-seating: building a character · BBC Bitesize / Drama Resource (~3 min)
exit: A. Return a faulty product — explain the problem in character
B. Voicemail explaining why you’re late
C. Talk-show intro — name, age, biggest want
resources: Breakout pairs · App. E Planning Template · App. F Hot-Seat prompts
notes: Appendix F hot-seat then App. E template. Model in role before pairs swap.

title: Finding Your Moment — Structure & Tension
walt: Combine elements of drama to shape and sustain a one-minute piece.
success: I can choose a key dramatic moment for my piece.
I can plan how tension builds across my piece.
brain: Where is the peak of your story?
What happens if you pause before the big line?
How can stillness create tension?

teach.title: One-minute structure (App. G)
teach.body: Opening line → build → turning point → final line. Show how tension, focus and contrast create interest across the minute.
teach.tip: Leave App. G on screen as a visual prompt students can refer back to.

teach.title: Pause + contrast
teach.body: Model how a pause and a contrast turn an ordinary line into the peak moment.
teach.tip: Same words twice: flat, then pause + contrast — difference in 30 sec.

sequence: Pairs create before/after freezes either side of a tense moment; partners guess what happened. Bring 2–3 back to show.
App. G: opening, build, turning point, final line + tension/focus/contrast.
Pairs: before/after tableau for each student’s own turning point; partner guesses the moment.
Model flat line vs paused/contrasted peak.
On App. E: opening line, how it builds, turning point (highest tension), final line. One suggestion per student.
Share a planned opening or final line + exit ticket. Preview Lesson 6 — devising words and voice.
model: Deliver one line flat, then again with a pause + contrast (loud → silent). Same words, very different tension.
watch: Building tension & using tableaux · Drama Resource / BBC Bitesize (~3 min)
exit: A. 30 seconds before opening a mysterious box
B. Countdown — narrate 30 sec before something huge
C. Waiting for news that could change everything
resources: Breakout pairs · App. E (continued) · App. G Structure Prompt Card

live_screens.title: Make the audience wait
live_screens.content_heading: Tension is more than being scary
content: Imagine you are home alone. The lights cut out. Something scrapes outside. Then: three slow knocks. What makes that tense?
Tension = uncertainty + waiting + important consequences. An actor controls it by delaying what the audience wants to know.
ideas: Pace · pause or silence · voice · body and eye focus · sound · delayed information
Say ‘There’s someone at the door’ once quickly and evenly, then again with stillness, a pause and a quiet final word. Name the exact difference.
schedule: Build the home-alone scene one detail at a time. Students show a 1–5 tension score in chat or on fingers.
Students identify the moment tension rose and the clue that caused it.
Name the formula and six tools. Compare the flat and shaped versions of the same line.
Everyone posts one precise choice-and-effect sentence.

iboard.label: iBoard check 1 · Choice and effect
iboard.prompt: Complete: The actor used ___, which made the audience ___ because ___. Name one exact moment—not just ‘it was good’.

live_screens.notes:
Evidence sweep

Scan for an acting choice and an audience effect. Prompt vague responses with: ‘What exactly changed?’ Cameras are optional throughout.

live_screens.title: Three frames, rising tension
live_screens.content_heading: Build a visual tension ladder
content: In a small group, create three freeze frames: 1 Normal → 2 A clue → 3 Almost revealed.
Choose one trigger: a bag moves · a note appears · a door opens · an object is missing. The audience should feel a clear rise without anyone explaining the story.
ideas: Actor · director/scribe · sound-maker · reporter. With two people, combine roles.
Describe the actor’s pose, choose the sound, write the three stage directions or report the group’s choices.
schedule: Choose the trigger and roles. The reporter opens a shared note.
Create Normal, Clue and Almost Revealed. Hold each frame for three seconds.
Add one sound or deliberate silence and strengthen the change in focus/body.
Reporter posts the group’s strongest change and its audience effect.

iboard.label: iBoard check 2 · Group evidence
iboard.prompt: Between Frame 1 and Frame 3 we changed ___. This increased tension because the audience ___.

live_screens.notes:
Room sweep

Visit briefly: ask ‘What changes across the three frames?’ Give one actionable note, then leave the group to revise.

live_screens.title: Structure the one-minute piece
live_screens.content_heading: Four beats give the minute a shape
content: Map your own monologue or soliloquy: opening → build → turning point → final line.
The turning point is the peak: a discovery, decision, confession or change. Aim to reach it around 40–50 seconds, then let the ending land.
ideas: Before the peak: quick speech or restless movement. At the peak: stillness, silence or one controlled line.
Compare a flat four-line version with one that delays the reveal. Students point to the opening, build, turn and final beat.
schedule: Teacher performs the flat and shaped versions; class identifies where tension peaks.
Write one short note or line for each of the four beats.
Stand or sit in role and rehearse only the build into the turning point twice.
Post the four beats and the technique that marks the peak.

iboard.label: iBoard check 3 · Structure map
iboard.prompt: Post: Opening / Build / Turning point / Final line. Add the tension tool you will use at the turning point.

live_screens.notes:
Keep it playable

Accept dot points rather than polished writing. The purpose is dramatic structure students can immediately rehearse.

live_screens.title: Test the turning point
live_screens.content_heading: Perform, receive one note, replay
content: Perform the 30–45 seconds around your turning point. Your partner watches for the moment tension peaks.
Directors give one note using: ‘When you used ___, the audience ___. Try ___ so that ___.’ Then replay the changed moment.
ideas: Performer first · director first; swap after the replay.
Read the script aloud, create sound, listen for vocal choices or direct the performance.
schedule: Choose performer/director and name the turning point.
Each performer tests the short section; director records one element-and-effect note.
Choose one exact change—pause, pace, focus, voice, body or sound.
Repeat the changed 10–20 seconds and compare the effect.
Post the change and save the plan to the folio.

iboard.label: iBoard check 4 · Exit evidence
iboard.prompt: I used ___ to make the audience ___. After feedback, I changed ___.

onenote.label: OneNote / folio · Drama L5
onenote.prompt: Save Structure and tension plan: character’s want · four beats · peak moment · three deliberate tension choices · feedback received · revision made.

live_screens.notes:
Lesson close

Use iBoard responses to identify students who can name element + effect and those who need a short structure conference in Lesson 6.

notes: Appendix G. Slow the turning point; use contrast and pause. Check in by room with one tip each.

title: Devising the Words & Voice
walt: Use improvisation to devise the words and voice for our piece.
success: I can improvise to find lines for my monologue or soliloquy.
I can use voice to show my character’s feelings.
wp: the feeling colour in your voice
how fast or slow you speak
how loud or soft you speak
brain: Which line would you keep from that improv?
How does pace change meaning?
Where should the voice match the turning point?

teach.title: Devising techniques (App. H)
teach.body: Solo devising: talk it out, partner thought-tracking, record & listen back. Demonstrate one live with a volunteer.
teach.tip: Keep the demo under two minutes — protect work time.

teach.title: Voice toolkit
teach.body: Tone, pace and volume show feeling — match the voice to the turning point.
teach.tip: Link voice choices explicitly to the App. G peak.

sequence: Same line — “Wait, look over there!” — in three voices/emotions. Quick whole-class unmuted round.
App. H techniques; demo one with a volunteer (<2 min).
Find and lock lines with a partner prompting/listening; note lines on App. E. Suggest a technique if stuck.
Solo: run start to finish once (even roughly) with voice choices applied.
Share one proud line + exit ticket. Preview rehearsal lessons.
model: “Talk it out” live for ~30 sec in role, then say which line you’d keep — modelling how devising works.
watch: Using your voice as an actor · National Theatre (~4 min)
exit: A. “We need to talk” three ways: scared, excited, furious
B. 30-sec rant in character about a tiny annoyance
C. Same line, two emotions — show the switch on camera
resources: Breakout pairs · App. H Devising Techniques · App. E Planning Template

live_screens.title: Voice makes subtext audible
live_screens.content_heading: The words stay; the meaning changes
content: Say ‘We need to talk’ as if you are excited, frightened and furious. The words are identical, but the listener receives three different stories.
Subtext is the meaning underneath the words. Actors reveal it through tone, pace, volume and pause.
ideas: Tone = feeling colour · pace = speed · volume = loud/soft · pause = chosen silence
Perform three versions. Students give each a tension score from 1–5 and identify the vocal evidence.
schedule: Whole class tries the same line three ways—aloud, on mute, or by annotating it.
Hear teacher versions and collect tension scores.
Name subtext and the four voice controls; link choices to character want.
Identify one exact change and what it communicated.

iboard.label: iBoard check 1 · Vocal evidence
iboard.prompt: The meaning changed when the actor changed ___ from ___ to ___. It suggested the character was ___.

live_screens.notes:
Listen for evidence

Students may perform muted and type their intended choices. The check is whether they can connect a vocal control to meaning.

live_screens.title: Talk it out to find the words
live_screens.content_heading: Do not write every word first
content: Performer speaks in character while the prompter asks: What do you want? What stops you? What can’t you say?
The scribe captures only the strongest three lines. Swap halfway. Rough, surprising language is useful; polished writing comes later.
ideas: Performer · prompter/scribe. The performer can speak, type or send short written answers.
Does the line reveal the want, obstacle, relationship or turning point? If not, let it go.
schedule: Choose roles and restate each character’s want and problem.
Prompt the first performer; capture three possible lines.
Swap and repeat for the second performer.
Each student chooses one line and explains why it belongs.

iboard.label: iBoard check 2 · Keep one line
iboard.prompt: My strongest improvised line is ‘___’. I kept it because it reveals ___ about the character or problem.

live_screens.notes:
Room prompt

If a pair stalls, ask one question in role and leave them with a 60-second speaking challenge. Do not turn this into silent script-writing.

live_screens.title: Build a voice ladder
live_screens.content_heading: Test the turning-point line three ways
content: Perform your key line three times. Change one control each time: tone, pace, volume or pause.
Your partner maps the choices, then names which version best serves the character and why. Create contrast between the moment before and the peak.
ideas: Before: quick + breathless → pause → Peak: slow + quiet
‘Version 2 worked because the pause made us wait for the confession.’
schedule: Select the turning-point line and decide the intended audience feeling.
Performer A tries three versions; partner maps and recommends one.
Performer B tests; partner maps and recommends.

iboard.label: iBoard check 3 · Before and peak
iboard.prompt: Before the turning point my voice is ___. At the peak it becomes ___. This makes the audience ___.

live_screens.notes:
Precision check

Ask students to replace emotion-only answers with audible controls: how fast, how loud, what tone and exactly where the silence falls.

live_screens.title: Build the rough full run
live_screens.content_heading: Turn discoveries into a playable piece
content: Arrange kept lines into opening → build → turning point → final line. Add short voice annotations such as [faster], [pause] or [quiet].
Run the whole piece once—even if it is imperfect. Listen to what feels repeated, unclear or too long; then cut or rewrite one part.
ideas: A complete rough journey with intentional voice—not a polished memorised script.
Perform live to yourself, time it and immediately jot what you noticed.
schedule: Place chosen lines into the four-beat structure.
Perform once from start to finish with voice choices.
Identify one unclear/repeated section and cut or rewrite it.
Post the strongest line/voice choice and save the rough script.

iboard.label: iBoard check 4 · Exit evidence
iboard.prompt: My strongest line is ‘___’. I will use ___ so it makes the audience ___. My next revision is ___.

onenote.label: OneNote / folio · Drama L6
onenote.prompt: Save Devised words and voice: rough script · highlight lines kept from improvisation · voice annotations · one cut/rewrite · a two-sentence reflection.

live_screens.notes:
End point

The piece should hang together end to end. Use iBoard to separate students needing line/structure help from those ready for camera work.

notes: Improvisation to find words and voice. Keep demos under two minutes. Piece should hang together end to end by the end of the lesson.

title: Performance Skills for the Camera
walt: Use performance skills suited to performing on camera.
success: I can project my voice clearly through the microphone.
I can use facial expression and the camera frame effectively.
wp: how much of you appears in the shot
where your eyes look on camera
small, clear moves that read on screen
brain: What ruins an otherwise great performance on camera?
Why does looking at the lens matter?
What one tip would you give a peer?

teach.title: On-camera skills
teach.body: Voice projection vs mic distance; facial expression close to camera; small clear gestures in frame; check background and lighting.
teach.tip: Model a less-effective then more-effective example side by side.

teach.title: Peer-tip protocol
teach.body: How to give one quick, specific tip on framing or voice — kind and concrete.
teach.tip: Ban vague “be better” — require one concrete action.

sequence: Check how much body is visible; tips on sitting/standing back, lighting, mic. Share 1–2 good framing examples.
Projection, expression, gestures, frame, light — less vs more effective model.
Several full runs using App. I checklist. On mute, cameras on; spotlights for quick tips.
Protocol for one kind, concrete tip.
Partners watch one run each; one tip on framing or voice.
Share one improvement + exit ticket. Action at least one feedback point before Lesson 8.
model: Same few lines twice: too far/flat/glancing away → good frame, eyes to lens, clear voice.
watch: Acting for camera — tips · StageMilk / BBC Bitesize (~4 min)
exit: A. Strongest 30 sec to camera — eyes to the lens
B. 30-sec news report in character
C. Close-up emotion change using just your face
resources: Breakout pairs · App. I Rehearsal Checklist

live_screens.title: The camera changes performance
live_screens.content_heading: Spot what weakens the performance
content: A strong performance can disappear if the actor is backlit, too far away, hard to hear, looking at their own preview or using gestures outside the frame.
Camera acting needs five checks: frame · light · lens focus · microphone · gesture size. Small, clear choices often read more strongly than stage-sized ones.
ideas: Show the same lines badly set up, then improved. Freeze after each change and ask what became clearer.
Use a plain wall or virtual background where allowed. No student must reveal a private room or turn on a camera.
schedule: Students inspect a deliberately weak setup and list likely problems.
Correct frame, light, eye line, sound and gesture one at a time.
Explain medium/close framing and why actors look near the lens.

iboard.label: iBoard check 1 · Technical diagnosis
iboard.prompt: List three faults and fixes: ‘The ___ is ___, so I would ___.’ Include at least one performance fix and one setup fix.

live_screens.notes:
Safeguard

Never ask students to pan around their home. Camera-off students analyse the teacher model and can demonstrate framing with a drawn rectangle.

live_screens.title: Find the frame that serves the story
live_screens.content_heading: Wide, medium or close?
content: Test three imagined or actual frames: wide for whole-body action, medium for gesture and face, close for thought and expression.
Choose the frame that best communicates your monologue—not simply the one that looks coolest.
ideas: Performer · director · tech/reporter. Rotate or combine roles.
Direct another performer, describe a safe setup, or draw and label the chosen shot.
schedule: Choose roles and identify the most important moment in the piece.
Try or mime wide, medium and close framing for the same lines.
Adjust headroom, eye line, light and mic distance.
Choose one frame and justify its dramatic effect.

iboard.label: iBoard check 2 · Frame decision
iboard.prompt: I chose a ___ shot because the audience needs to notice ___. I adjusted ___ so that ___.

live_screens.notes:
Room sweep

Check that choices are story-led. Ask: ‘What should the audience notice at this distance?’

live_screens.title: Micro-performance lab
live_screens.content_heading: Improve twenty seconds, not everything
content: Perform the 20 seconds around the turning point. Test four camera-sized skills: lens focus, clear projection, readable facial expression and one controlled gesture.
The director gives one concrete action. Replay the same section immediately so both people can compare.
ideas: ‘Keep your eyes near the lens during the pause so the audience stays with the decision.’
Read aloud for vocal feedback, listen as director, or annotate a script with eye line and gesture cues.
schedule: Each performer shares once; director notes one observable issue.
Apply the note and repeat the same moment.
Record what changed and the audience effect.

iboard.label: iBoard check 3 · Before and after
iboard.prompt: First, ___ weakened the moment. I changed ___. The replay was stronger because ___.

live_screens.notes:
Make feedback observable

Accept ‘move the camera closer’ or ‘slow the key line’; reject personality judgements such as ‘be more confident’ unless converted to an action.

live_screens.title: Make a 30-second camera take
live_screens.content_heading: Set up, perform, watch back, revise
content: Complete a safe technical check, then capture one uninterrupted 30-second take. Watch or listen to the whole clip before judging it.
Score voice · face · frame · gesture out of three: 1 not clear yet · 2 mostly clear · 3 deliberate and effective. Choose only one next action.
ideas: Perform live, ask a partner to score the four areas, or use an audio-only rehearsal.
A labelled setup diagram is valid evidence; no screenshot needs to show personal surroundings.
schedule: Use App. I: safe background, frame, light, sound, lens focus.
Perform the strongest 30 seconds without stopping.
Watch/listen once and score the four performance areas.
Name one action and save rehearsal evidence.

iboard.label: iBoard check 4 · Exit evidence
iboard.prompt: My camera strength is ___; evidence: ___. My next action is ___.

onenote.label: OneNote / folio · Drama L7
onenote.prompt: Save Camera rehearsal evidence: setup checklist · voice/face/frame/gesture scores · feedback · screenshot OR labelled setup diagram · next action.

live_screens.notes:
Diagnostic close

Sort responses into performance, setup and access needs so Lesson 8 feedback pairs can be purposeful.

notes: Model less-effective then more-effective side by side. Circulate via spotlight during solo rehearsals.

title: Rehearsal & Peer Feedback
walt: Refine our performance using peer feedback and explain how we used elements of drama.
success: I can give a helpful comment using drama vocabulary.
I can explain one element of drama used in my piece.
wp: specific, kind comments that help refine
one of the 10 drama building blocks
what the choice makes the audience feel
improve a small part with intention
brain: What makes feedback useful?
Which element did you use on purpose?
What will you change after today?

teach.title: Feedback language (App. J)
teach.body: Recap specific, kind feedback using elements-of-drama vocabulary and App. J sentence starters.
teach.tip: Model vague “good job” vs specific element feedback so the difference is clear.

teach.title: Explain your elements
teach.body: How to say, in one sentence, which element you used and what effect it had — folio evidence language.
teach.tip: Bring App. A back on screen for vocabulary.

sequence: Vocal & physical warm-up + tongue-twister. Short and energetic before peer performing.
App. J + App. A — specific vs vague feedback.
Pairs perform; listener completes App. J sheet; swap; final adjustments. Check sheets are completed.
Write the explanation + one final tweak from feedback (folio evidence).
Volunteer shares feedback they’ll use + exit ticket. Pieces close to final before Week 9.
model: Two comments on the same performance: vague “good job” vs “the pause before your final line really built the tension.” Ask which helps more.
watch: A powerful short monologue — spot the elements · teacher-selected (~2 min)
exit: A. Re-record your turning point after today’s feedback
B. Director’s note to self — what you improved and why
C. Final line three different ways
resources: Breakout pairs · App. J Peer Feedback Sheet · App. A Elements reference

live_screens.title: Feedback must cause a change
live_screens.content_heading: Kind, specific and usable
content: Compare: ‘Good job!’ with ‘The pause before the confession built tension; hold it two seconds longer.’ Only one gives the performer an action.
Use the feedback formula: notice the element → explain its effect → suggest an exact action.
ideas: Name an element that worked and the audience effect it created.
Suggest one small, observable action—not ‘be better’ or ‘have confidence’.
Tension · focus · contrast · mood · voice · movement · space · symbol
schedule: Vote for the comment that would actually improve a performance and explain why.
Model notice + effect + action using a short performed line.
Turn two vague comments into director-quality notes.

iboard.label: iBoard check 1 · Upgrade the note
iboard.prompt: Upgrade ‘Speak better’: I noticed ___, which made the audience ___. Try ___ so that ___.

live_screens.notes:
Evidence sweep

Look for drama vocabulary plus a doable action. Read two anonymous responses aloud and improve them together.

live_screens.title: Peer rehearsal: round one
live_screens.content_heading: One performer, one director, then swap
content: Share your one-minute piece—or your strongest 45 seconds if it is unfinished. The director uses Appendix J to capture one glow and one grow.
Feedback must refer to something that happened: the line, pause, focus, voice, expression, movement or framing.
ideas: Performer A / director B, then swap. Keep time firmly.
Perform by audio, read the script, listen as director or give feedback from a written excerpt.
schedule: Open App. J, choose order and tell the director what feedback is most needed.
First performance and one-minute spoken feedback.
Each student writes the most useful note received or given.

iboard.label: iBoard check 2 · Peer note
iboard.prompt: One specific note was: ___. It is useful because the performer can ___.

live_screens.notes:
Teacher sweep

Check that both students perform or contribute evidence. Prompt directors to name the audience effect, not simply the actor’s behaviour.

live_screens.title: Prove the feedback changed something
live_screens.content_heading: Revise the highest-value moment
content: Choose the one note most likely to improve meaning for the audience. Apply it to a 10–20 second moment, then replay that exact section.
Compare before and after using element + effect language. A revision is successful only when it changes what the audience notices, understands or feels.
ideas: Strengthen a turning point, clarify the character’s want, or make the final line land.
Before: rushed confession. Revision: pause and stillness. Effect: audience anticipates the truth.
schedule: Underline one peer note and state the intended effect.
Show the partner; partner compares before and after.
Post the exact revision and changed effect.

iboard.label: iBoard check 3 · Before and after
iboard.prompt: Before, I ___. I revised ___. This changed the audience effect from ___ to ___.

live_screens.notes:
Keep the loop short

Do not allow a full rewrite. Students need to experience feedback → action → visible improvement within this block.

live_screens.title: Lock the two improvements
live_screens.content_heading: One full run with deliberate choices
content: Perform the whole piece once. Use Appendix I to check voice, character, structure, tension and camera choices.
Lock two improvements you will keep next lesson. Do not chase ten tiny fixes; choose the changes that most help the audience.
ideas: Can I name where each improvement appears and what it does?
Piece runs end to end; feedback is recorded; remaining priority is specific.
schedule: Mark two revised moments and choose a feedback focus.
Perform without stopping; partner or self uses App. I.
Record two improvements that will stay and one remaining priority.
Post evidence and save the peer-feedback record.

iboard.label: iBoard check 4 · Exit evidence
iboard.prompt: The feedback I acted on was ___. It improved ___ by ___. My remaining priority is ___.

onenote.label: OneNote / folio · Drama L8
onenote.prompt: Save Rehearsal and peer feedback: peer comment · exact revision · element-and-effect explanation · before/after reflection · remaining priority.

live_screens.notes:
End point

Use the four iBoard posts plus App. J to identify who revised from evidence and who still needs teacher-directed feedback.

notes: Appendix A vocabulary again. Check feedback sheets are completed — this feeds the folio.

title: Independent Preparation
walt: Finalise and polish our piece, ready for filming.
success: I can perform my piece confidently from memory.
I know how I will film and submit my piece.
wp: send the finished film by the agreed method
brain: What still needs polishing?
Where will you film, and how will you light it?
What question will you bring to the help room?

teach.title: Goal + Filming Guide (App. K)
teach.body: Finalise and rehearse. Share App. K filming & submission guide: landscape, light, frame, quiet, one full take, watch back.
teach.tip: Pin App. K in the chat for the whole lesson.

teach.title: Whole-class readiness Q&A
teach.body: Show of hands on readiness; troubleshoot common tech questions (orientation, file size, upload) together.
teach.tip: Answer FAQs once for everyone to save independent time.

sequence: Goal + App. K on screen and pinned in chat.
Rehearse on camera; fine-tune lines/movement; optional help-room check-ins one at a time.
Confirm due date for Lesson 10 + exit ticket. Send a written reminder after class.
model: Walk App. K checklist aloud: landscape · face a window · upper body in frame · quiet · one full take · watch back.
watch: A student monologue performance · teacher-selected example (~2 min)
exit: A. Opening 30 sec — no script, one take
B. Confidence take in your actual filming spot
C. Best-framing test — strongest 30 sec, well lit
resources: App. I Rehearsal Checklist · App. K Filming & Submission Guide · help breakout

live_screens.title: Pass the five readiness gates
live_screens.content_heading: Independent does not mean invisible
content: Rate each gate green, amber or red: 1 complete structure · 2 about one minute · 3 lines secure enough · 4 drama choices deliberate · 5 safe filming setup possible.
A red or amber rating is useful evidence when it names the exact repair. Choose the gate that most affects the whole performance.
ideas: Mostly ready; one specific repair needed.
Blocked or incomplete; ask for targeted help now.
schedule: Open script, App. I and App. K; locate the latest feedback.
Rate all five gates and write one piece of evidence for each.
Choose the highest-impact amber/red gate and one repair action.
Post current status so teacher can form the help room.

iboard.label: iBoard check 1 · Readiness status
iboard.prompt: My priority gate is ___ and it is green/amber/red. Evidence: ___. I will repair it by ___.

live_screens.notes:
Build the help queue

Sort iBoard responses into structure, performance and technology/access. Invite red students first; do not wait for them to self-nominate again.

live_screens.title: Targeted rehearsal sprint
live_screens.content_heading: Repeat the moments that matter
content: Avoid ten unfocused full runs. Rehearse: opening ×2 · turning point ×3 · final line ×2, then perform one uninterrupted full run.
Time the full run. Around one minute is the goal, but meaning matters more than racing to fit.
ideas: Focus, character and a reason to keep watching.
Clear peak with deliberate contrast or tension.
Land it; hold focus for a beat before relaxing.
schedule: Mark the opening, turning point and final line.
Run the three moments using the 2–3–2 pattern.
Perform once without stopping and record the duration.
Name the strongest and weakest moment.

iboard.label: iBoard check 2 · Timed evidence
iboard.prompt: My full run was ___ seconds. Strongest moment: ___ because ___. Weakest moment: ___.

live_screens.notes:
Visible independence

The timed response is a checkpoint, not a competition. Follow up implausible times or missing weakest moments with a quick conference.

live_screens.title: Solve one real problem
live_screens.content_heading: Choose the right support lane
content: Choose one lane: structure (the story is unclear) · voice/tension (the peak is flat) · camera/tech (setup or submission problem).
Bring one question, test one piece of advice, then report the result. Students who are green can act as peer directors or continue targeted rehearsal.
ideas: What changes between the opening and final line?
Which exact control will make the peak different?
What is the safest simple setup or approved fallback?
schedule: State one problem as a question and join the relevant help group.
Teacher/peer gives one action; student records it.
Try the affected moment or setup immediately.
Post problem, advice, action and result.

iboard.label: iBoard check 3 · Help acted on
iboard.prompt: Problem: ___. Advice: ___. I tried ___. The result was ___.

live_screens.notes:
Access

Keep a written queue. For technology blockers, agree on an approved fallback rather than repeatedly troubleshooting the same device.

live_screens.title: Make a finalisation contract
live_screens.content_heading: Finish with evidence and a concrete next step
content: Complete one final uninterrupted rehearsal and recheck Appendices I and K. Then plan where, when, device and submission method without showing or describing private spaces publicly.
Choose the final two actions that must happen before filming. If blocked, name the person or approved school pathway that can help.
ideas: A simple labelled setup—light in front, device stable, quiet background—is enough.
Green means evidence-backed readiness, not optimism.
schedule: Perform without stopping and notice whether the earlier repair held.
Recheck performance and filming readiness using I/K.
Record setup, timing, device, submission and fallback.
Post status and save the final readiness record.

iboard.label: iBoard check 4 · Final status
iboard.prompt: I am green/amber/red for filming because ___. My next exact action is ___.

onenote.label: OneNote / folio · Drama L9
onenote.prompt: Save Final readiness record: script status · duration · deliberate elements · safe setup diagram/checklist · help used · final two actions and fallback.

live_screens.notes:
After class

Contact amber/red students using the normal school process. The lesson now leaves four checkpoints instead of a forty-minute invisible work block.

notes: Appendix K. Keep a help breakout open as a virtual queue (raise hand / chat). Weeks 9–10 are long DO by design.

title: Final Rehearsal, Filming & Reflection
walt: Perform our final piece with confidence and reflect on our drama journey.
success: I can perform my piece and sustain my character for one minute.
I can explain how I used elements of drama and what my piece communicates.
wp: keep character and focus for the full minute
think back on what you learned
who your piece is speaking to
brain: What are you most proud of?
Which element did the most work in your piece?
What would you try differently next time?

teach.title: Final filming tips
teach.body: Good light, quiet room, one full take with no stopping, watch the recording back before submitting. Reconfirm exact submission method and deadline.
teach.tip: Keep the App. K checklist on screen during the film block.

sequence: Individual vocal & physical warm-up on camera — stretches, breathing, tongue-twister. Guide whole-class to settle nerves.
Final rehearsals; film the one-minute piece; submit via agreed method. Help breakout open.
Whole-class return — how it felt (chat or aloud). Keep it light.
Reflection Sheet (App. L) for the folio — elements used + what the piece communicates. May finish as homework.
model: Reconfirm: quiet · landscape · light · upper body · one full take · watch back before submit.
watch: How to film yourself well at home — framing, light & sound (~3 min)
exit: A. Favourite 30 sec of your final piece
B. Reflection: the moment you’re proudest of
C. Director’s wrap speech — thank your “cast and crew”
resources: App. K · App. L Reflection Sheet · agreed submission method · help breakout

live_screens.title: Prepare the performer and space
live_screens.content_heading: Calm body, clear voice, safe setup
content: Warm up without exhausting the performance: release shoulders and jaw, breathe low and steady, hum, then speak the opening and final line clearly.
Use Appendix K for a final frame · light · sound · device · privacy check. Fix only what will materially help the audience.
ideas: Slow the exhale, plant your feet and focus on the character’s want.
No public tour of the filming space. Use the approved background, audio/fallback or school support arrangement.
schedule: Guided physical release, breathing, humming and articulation.
Speak opening and final line with clear focus and breath.
Complete App. K and solve one setup issue.
Post readiness and the final fix.

iboard.label: iBoard check 1 · Ready state
iboard.prompt: I am green/amber/red. My final setup or performance fix is ___, because ___.

live_screens.notes:
Teacher action

Move red responses straight to the help pathway. Keep the emotional tone calm: this is a readiness check, not a public judgement.

live_screens.title: One uninterrupted dress rehearsal
live_screens.content_heading: Finish the take before judging it
content: Perform the full piece without restarting for small mistakes. Watch or listen back once from beginning to end.
Choose one high-value revision: the change that most improves clarity, character or audience effect. Endless restarting usually makes the work less focused, not more.
ideas: Was the character sustained? Did the turning point peak? Did the final line land?
Make one precise adjustment, rehearse that moment once, then move on.
schedule: Silence notifications, open the checklist and settle into character.
Watch/listen once; record duration and strongest element.
Rehearse the highest-value adjustment once and report it.

iboard.label: iBoard check 2 · Dress-run evidence
iboard.prompt: Duration: ___ seconds. Strongest element: ___, shown when ___. My one fix is ___.

live_screens.notes:
Protect filming time

At 30 minutes, students move forward. Perfectionism is not evidence of readiness; a complete reviewed take is.

live_screens.title: Capture and verify the final performance
live_screens.content_heading: A file is not finished until it is checked
content: Film the one-minute monologue or soliloquy using the agreed method. A second take is optional only if time allows and you know the exact reason.
Watch the complete chosen file, use the required filename, then submit. If blocked, stop repeating the failed step and enter the help pathway with the exact error.
ideas: Correct file · complete beginning/end · audible · visible if video required · opens successfully.
Submitted · uploading · blocked. All three require honest evidence.
schedule: Confirm storage, filename, submission location and fallback.
Film one complete performance; optional purposeful second take.
Watch the chosen file from start to finish.
Upload and post status or the exact blocker.

iboard.label: iBoard check 3 · Submission tracker
iboard.prompt: Status: submitted / uploading / blocked. Evidence or exact blocker: ___. Next action (if needed): ___.

live_screens.notes:
Teacher dashboard

Use this response as the live submission sweep. Follow school privacy and storage rules; never request public links or personal cloud access.

live_screens.title: Name the growth, not just the grade
live_screens.content_heading: What did your choices communicate?
content: Return together. Share one word for how performing felt; viewing selected clips is optional and follows class consent and privacy expectations.
Complete Appendix L using element + evidence + effect. Compare your work with Lesson 5: what can you now shape deliberately that you could not shape then?
ideas: ‘I used stillness before the final line, which focused the audience on the decision.’
‘Since Lesson 5, I can build tension across four clear beats instead of relying on loudness.’
schedule: One-word chat check-in; acknowledge persistence and problem-solving.
Identify three drama elements with exact performance evidence and audience effect.
Compare the final work with the Lesson 5 structure/tension plan.
Post the proud moment and next goal; save the final folio reflection.

iboard.label: iBoard check 4 · Final exit
iboard.prompt: I am proud of ___. My use of ___ made the audience ___. Next time I will ___.

onenote.label: OneNote / folio · Drama L10
onenote.prompt: Save Final reflection: what the piece communicates · three elements with evidence/effect · growth since Lesson 5 · strongest moment · next performance goal.

live_screens.notes:
Close the evidence loop

Follow up any blocked submission after class. Assessment evidence now includes the performance plus six lessons of choices, revisions and reflection.

notes: Celebrate first — then App. L reflection for the folio. Filming checklist from App. K stays visible.
